fact_text: Sign languages are used by Deaf communities around the world; sign languages are not universal.
BSL and Austrailian Sign Language (Auslan) share historical links. ASL developed separately and is quite different from BSL.
Each sign language has its own vocabulary and grammar; knowing one does not mean you can automatically understand another.
The British Sign Language Act became law on 28 April 2022 and recognises BSL in England, Wales and Scotland.
BSL is a natural language with its own grammar and vocabulary, not English represented on the hands.
Some people use capital-D Deaf for a cultural and linguistic identity; not every deaf person identifies this way.
BSL has regional variation: signs can differ between places and communities.
An estimate cited in the BSL Act explanatory notes is about 87,000 BSL users in England; it is a language-use estimate, not a count of everyone with hearing loss.
Access to Work may help eligible people with costs such as communication support at work.
Facial expression, eyebrows, head movement and mouth patterns can contribute grammatical information in BSL.
Some Deaf people face barriers to mental health support when services are not available accessibly in sign language.
Signed languages express humour and emotion through timing, movement, facial expression and visual storytelling.
The 1880 Milan Congress promoted oral education and opposed sign language in schools, harming sign-language education in many places.
The first international Deaf sports games were held in Paris in 1924; they became the Deaflympics.
Signers can use locations and movement in signing space to talk about time and events.
Signers can establish people or objects in signing space and refer back to those locations.
Deaf performers use character shifts, body movement and facial expression in storytelling and theatre.
BSL has its own systematic grammar; it is not a shortened form of English.
Hearing dogs can be trained to alert Deaf people to everyday sounds such as a doorbell or alarm.
Hearing Dogs for Deaf People was established in 1982.
Signing space can show where different people or animals are and refer back to them.
Audio-only travel announcements can mean Deaf passengers miss delays, platform changes or safety information.
Visual boards, text alerts and clear signs make travel information easier to access.
Waving within someone’s view or a gentle tap can get attention; preferences differ between people.
More than 90% of deaf children are born to hearing parents. This means they are often the only deaf person in their family.
CODA means "Child of Deaf Adult(s)". Although CODAs are hearing, their first language may be sign language.  They may be expected to interpret for their parent(s) from a young age.
A sign name can identify someone without fingerspelling their full name each time.
In many Deaf communities, sign names are given by Deaf people rather than chosen by a hearing learner; practices vary.
The British Deaf Association was founded in 1890 and has campaigned for Deaf rights and sign-language recognition.
Deaf clubs have historically been important for social connection, shared language and community organising.
Deaf culture and language are shared through families, friendships, schools, clubs and community events.
Dim lighting, background noise and staff facing away can make communication harder for Deaf customers.
Deaf friends may meet in cafés and restaurants to socialise in sign language.
Lipreading is difficult: many speech sounds look alike on the lips, and some are not visible. Context helps but cannot make every conversation clear.
Visual or vibrating alerts can provide access to some household sounds, such as doorbells and alarms.
The Deaflympics began in 1924 and are an international sports event for Deaf athletes.
Deaf people experience music in varied ways, including through hearing, vibration, signed performance or dance.
BSL uses depicting constructions to show features such as shape, position or movement.
Video calls can let BSL users communicate directly over distance.
Signing space can show how objects relate or move without naming each one repeatedly.
Visual attention helps signers follow a conversation; look at the signer and their face, not only their hands.
Pauses, gaze and other visual cues can help show turn-taking in signed conversations.
Learning BSL also means learning about Deaf culture, identity and communication preferences.
